title: Why the Dragon exists: ...g6, the bishop on g7 and the pawn on d6
outcomes: Explains in own words why Black answers 5.Nc3 with ...g6: the long diagonal for the bishop, with the d6 pawn and the c-file as the setting that makes it work, and what ...g6 costs
Predicts how far a bishop on g7 sees when the diagonal holds a knight, a pawn or nothing
Steps through the first six moves and says what each is for
Says why 6.e5 does not refute ...g6, and reads opening counts as results of games, not verdicts

The c-file is half-open for Black and the d-file half-open for White.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: once Black's bishop reaches g7, what do you think it aims at, and what stands in its way first?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Why does Black answer 5.Nc3 with ...g6, and what do the bishop on g7 and the pawn on d6 make possible for the whole game? By the end you will explain it in your own words and could teach it to a friend. Marks you will meet: [H] is a hypothesis (a guess worth testing), [I] an inference (reasoned, not proven), [V] checked here.

**Three ways to answer 5.Nc3.** [I] 5...a6 keeps every plan open and stops Bb5 and Nb5, but commits to nothing. 5...Nc6 develops and hits d4, but gives the c-pawn's file plan less clarity. 5...g6 prepares Bg7: a clear plan and a clear diagonal, at a price, shown on the next card. So the reason for ...g6 is the diagonal; the d6 pawn and the c-file are the setting in which it works.

steps.prompt: Before the boards: which of the three answers to 5.Nc3 would you pick, and what do you think it gives up?

steps.text: **What ...g6 costs.** [I] Three prices. The light squares around the king (f6, h6) rely on the g7 bishop. The king depends on that one bishop, so trading it is White's regular plan. And the bishop needs time: ...a6 or ...Nc6 develop faster. [I] The gain, a strong long diagonal, outweighs these prices only while the diagonal stays open.

steps.text: **What decided the range?** Not the bishop, which stood on the same square in all three. What stood on the diagonal decided it: nothing of Black's own, a white pawn on e5, a white knight on d4. Capablanca noted that the bishop is usually stronger than the knight except in blocked positions [V-sheet 8.4]. [I] With its diagonal blocked, the Dragon bishop loses that edge.

**Idea 1: the long diagonal.** Play ...g6 and the bishop can go to g7, from where it looks through f6, e5, d4 and c3 to b2 and a1. It is a distant centre-control piece, influencing the middle without a pawn there: a thought the hypermodern school pushed [S].

steps.caption: Black's bishop arrives on g7. Its own knight on f6 is first in line, then White's knight on d4.

line.say: The g6 pawn made room; from g7 the bishop looks down the long diagonal toward b2.

White's knight stands on d4, the second piece.

steps.text: **Idea 2: the pawn on d6.** It guards e5 and c5, so a white pawn on e5 can be captured, and it keeps White's e-pawn from advancing for free. It is not on the long diagonal, so it blocks nothing there. [I] It also fixes Black's centre until ...d5 becomes possible.

steps.caption: The pawn on d6 watches e5 and c5. White's e4 pawn would like to advance; the pawn stands guard.

claims.statement: Black's pieces attack e5 (the d6 pawn).
White has no piece attacking e5 yet.

steps.text: **Idea 3: the half-open c-file.** After ...cxd4 Black has no pawn on the c-file, but White's c2 pawn is still there. A black rook on c8 would press on that file and on the knight on c3. [I] In most Dragon games Black's rook pressure goes down this file, because White's c-pawn is the only pawn left on it. The d-file is White's: White has no d-pawn, Black has d6.

steps.caption: After the knight trade on d4 the c-file is open to Black's rook on c8, and White's knight on c3 stands in front of its c2 pawn. [I] This is why Black's rook often goes to c8.

claims.statement: The c-file is half-open for Black, the d-file for White.
One black piece (the rook on c8) attacks c3.

steps.text: **The first six moves, with reasons.** A move order is a chain of small purposes. Emanuel Lasker pointed out that first moves leave lasting marks on a game [V-sheet 1.12]; he used the French as his example, and we borrow the idea. Watch what each move leaves behind. Step through the boards and say each purpose aloud before reading it.

steps.caption: Move 1. Why not copy with ...e5? [I] After ...c5 White cannot build a pawn centre on d4 and e4 for free: the c-pawn is traded for White's d-pawn, which gives Black a half-open file. ...e5 would leave Black's e5 pawn needing protection at once.

Guards e5 and c5 and opens the road for the bishop. Leaves behind: a pawn on d6 that fixes the centre.
White challenges the c5 pawn and opens the centre.

steps.text: **Who plays the Dragon, and why?** Our data: after 5.Nc3, 5...g6 was reached in 1436 of 6,673 games in the 2100+ online band, and in 100 of 328 in the 1100-1300 band (a small sample). In our master file 720 of 12,442 games after 5.Nc3 continue 5...g6; 5...a6 has 9,815. [H] The Dragon has a reputation as a sharp, risk-taking choice, and its plan is easy to see (a diagonal and a file); counts cannot test either.

steps.text: **Counts are results, not verdicts.** The 579 games with 6.Be3 only show that strong players chose it often. A move can be popular for fashion, preparation or style. The engine here agrees that 6.Be3 is a good move (it is within 40 cp of the top choice at depth 16), but the count did not tell us that. Check the claim, not the crowd.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The pawn on g6 lets the bishop reach g7 and look down the long diagonal; what stands on that diagonal decides its range. The d6 pawn guards e5, so a white e-pawn push can be met by a capture. The c-file is half-open for Black, the d-file for White. ...g6 costs light-square weakness and a dependence on the g7 bishop. Counts show what was chosen, not what is best. Next lesson: the pawn structure and the breaks.

**Typical mistakes.** [I] First, grabbing the e4 pawn with the knight: after 6.Be3 the capture ...Nxe4 loses a piece for a pawn, because White recaptures (see the board). Second, letting the bishop be traded on h6 with no plan for the king. Third, blocking your own bishop with a knight that never moves, so the diagonal stays closed.

steps.caption: 6...Nxe4? is a mistake: White's knight on c3 recaptures and Black has given up a knight for a pawn.

line.say: Tempting: it wins a pawn for one move.
White recaptures; Black has lost a knight for a pawn.

claims.statement: 6...Nxe4 scores at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **Say it like this.** [I] 'Black plays ...g6 so the bishop can sit on g7 and look along the long diagonal. It works while nothing stands on that diagonal, and it fails when a white pawn on e5 blocks it. Set up a bishop on g7 with a pawn on e5 and count its squares. Warning: do not grab the e4 pawn with the knight; White just recaptures.'
